articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran-Related Designations, General Licenses, and Amends FAQs; Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and issued Iran General License GG, 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving Karnakis and Karnakis,' and Iran General License HH, 'Authorizing Wind Down Activities, Limited Safety and Environmental Transactions, and the Offloading of Cargo Involving Certain Persons or Vessels Blocked on October 21, 2026.' These actions are part of ongoing efforts to address Iran's illicit activities.

Additionally, OFAC issued Russia-related General License 131K, 'Authorizing Certain Transactions for the Negotiation of and Entry Into Contingent Contracts for the Sale of Lukoil International GmbH and Related Maintenance Activities.' The agency also amended Frequently Asked Questions 1224 and 1225.

In a significant development, OFAC removed several individuals and entities from its Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List related to Belarus and North Korea. This includes the removal of Andrei Rybakou, CEO of Belaruskali, from the SDN list.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). This action targets individuals and entities deemed to be involved in activities that undermine American intellectual property.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC has also issued associated General Licenses to provide guidance and authorization for certain transactions that might otherwise be prohibited. These licenses aim to mitigate unintended consequences while upholding the integrity of the sanctions program.

The PAIPA designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating intellectual property theft and protecting American innovation on a global scale. Further details on the specific individuals and entities designated, as well as the scope of the General Licenses, are available on the OFAC website.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ for Earthquake Relief
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License (GL 60A), 'Authorizing Transactions Related to Earthquake Relief Efforts in Venezuela.' This amendment replaces and supersedes the previous GL 60.

The primary change in GL 60A is the extension of the authorization period for earthquake relief efforts, moving the expiration date from October 23, 2026, to April 21, 2027. This extension aims to ensure continued humanitarian assistance to Venezuela.

In conjunction with the amended General License, OFAC has also updated Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) 1263 to reflect the extended authorization end date, providing clarity for those involved in relief operations.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Sanctions Cuban Bank, and Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, targeting entities involved in the Iranian regime's abuse of religious charity networks and its international financial networks and shadow banking architecture. This action is part of 'Operation Economic Outcast' to intensify economic pressure on Iran.

In a separate action, OFAC, in coordination with the Department of State, sanctioned Banco Internacional de Comercio, S.A. (BICSA), a Cuban state-owned bank. BICSA was designated for operating in the financial services sector of the Cuban economy, with the State Department noting its provision of services to Karafarin Bank, an Iranian financial institution previously sanctioned by the U.S.

Additionally, OFAC issued Russia-related General License 128D, 'Authorizing Certain Transactions Involving Lukoil Retail Service Stations Located Outside of Russia,' and Russia-related General License 130B, 'Authorizing Transactions Involving Certain Lukoil Entities in Bulgaria.' Iran-related General License FF, 'Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance,' was also issued, along with a new Cuba-related FAQ 1276 and an amended Russia-related FAQ 1225.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Prominent Venezuelan Politician Jorge Rodriguez from Sanctions List
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has removed Jorge Rodriguez, the head of Venezuela's National Assembly, from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list. This delisting ends the associated asset freeze and removes obstacles for U.S. persons attempting to deal with him.

Rodriguez, who has led the Venezuelan legislature since 2021, was initially designated in 2018. His removal from the sanctions list signals ongoing U.S. efforts to pursue stability in Venezuela amid further opening of Venezuela's energy sector and progress towards a potential political transition.

This action follows earlier sanctions relief for interim President Delcy Rodriguez and other members of the Maduro inner circle, underscoring a shift in Washington's approach from economic warfare to diplomatic engagement and expanded energy investment in Venezuela.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Al Jazeera / Reuters

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial networks and operations that pose a threat to U.S. national security.

The designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating global illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing. These measures typically involve freezing assets and prohibiting U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with the designated parties.

Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated, as well as the reasons for their inclusion on the sanctions list, are available on the OFAC website. These actions are part of a broader strategy to protect the international financial system from abuse.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics; Designates International Criminal Court Officials
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics for alleged violations of sanctions regulations. The details of the settlement, including the specific violations and the agreed-upon penalty, are available in the enforcement information.

In a separate action, OFAC designated officials of the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued associated General Licenses. This move follows previous U.S. concerns regarding the ICC's actions and jurisdiction.
Additionally, OFAC announced the removal of a Burma-related designation. This removal signifies a change in circumstances or policy regarding the previously sanctioned individual or entity in Burma.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued a new Russia-related General License. This license, GL 135, authorizes certain transactions related to imports of Russian diesel fuel to the U.S. until April 7, 2027.

This action provides specific authorizations for activities that would otherwise be prohibited under existing Russia sanctions programs. General Licenses are typically issued to allow for certain humanitarian, administrative, or other specific types of transactions.
The issuance of this General License reflects ongoing adjustments to the U.S. sanctions framework concerning Russia, aiming to balance economic pressure with other policy considerations.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations and Issues General Licenses for Iran and Russia
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' targeting Iran's shadow fleet network. These actions aim to intensify pressure on the Iranian regime's illicit financial activities.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC has issued an Iran-related General License, providing specific authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited. This aims to mitigate unintended consequences while maintaining the effectiveness of the sanctions.

Additionally, OFAC has issued an amended Russia-related General License. This amendment reflects ongoing adjustments to the U.S. sanctions policy concerning Russia, likely to address specific operational or humanitarian considerations.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: EU Adopts 22nd Sanctions Package Against Russia, Designating 1,569 Individuals and Entities
body: The European Union adopted its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia on October 12, 2026, adding 1,569 individuals and entities to its sanctions lists. This brings the total number of designations under the Ukraine-related sanctions regime to almost 4,600.

The latest package is primarily a listings package, targeting companies forming part of Russia's military-industrial complex, including businesses involved in the production and supply of components used in missiles, drones, military aircraft, and related defense technologies.

The measures were adopted in response to Russia's continuing aggression against Ukraine and recent attacks on civilian infrastructure. The package has been implemented through Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/2279 and Council Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2281.
articles.source: Council of the European Union / Euronews

articles.headline: EU Sanctions North Korean and Russian Targets for Supporting DPRK Weapons Programs
body: The Council of the European Union adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK). These designations target those responsible for supporting, promoting, or facilitating activities contributing to the DPRK's nuclear weapons, ballistic missiles, or other weapons of mass destruction programs, as well as for violating and evading United Nations sanctions.

The new listings specifically target activities linked to the growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, including the deployment of DPRK workers in Russia, commercial and industrial cooperation, and the 'arms-for-oil' trade, all in violation of UN Security Council prohibitions.

Among those listed is Ri Song Jin, a researcher at the DPRK National Aerospace Technology Administration and an official at the DPRK Missile General Bureau, who has been deployed to Russia as a technician supporting Russia's use of DPRK missiles. The Council also listed Russian real estate development company Samolet Group and its CEO, Anna Nikolaevna Akinshina.
articles.source: Council of the European Union / NK News

articles.headline: UK Expands Russia Sanctions, Targeting Energy, Evasion Networks, and Military Support
body: The UK introduced a further package of Russia-related sanctions measures on October 8, 2026, comprising 38 new designations. These measures demonstrate a continued focus on Russia's energy revenues, sanctions circumvention networks, and shadow fleet activities.

The new designations target Russian oil companies, shadow fleet tankers, payment platforms, crypto-exchanges, and entities involved in the procurement, manufacture, and transport of goods supporting Russia's military-industrial base.
This action combines new listings with a particular emphasis on maritime, energy, and financial enforcement, complementing the EU's recent designations-focused package.
articles.source: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office / Reuters

articles.headline: Global Markets React to Intensifying Russian Attacks in Ukraine and Middle East Crisis
body: Global markets are exhibiting volatility in response to intensifying long-range Russian attacks across Ukraine, which have caused significant civilian casualties. The ongoing conflict continues to fuel uncertainty in energy and commodity markets.

Adding to market anxieties is the persistent Middle Eastern crisis, including renewed Yemeni offensives and the Gaza war. These geopolitical tensions contribute to a risk-off sentiment among investors, impacting global equities and safe-haven assets.

Analysts are closely monitoring developments in both regions, as the interconnectedness of global supply chains and energy markets means that prolonged instability could have far-reaching economic consequences.

articles.headline: Oil Prices Surge Amidst Graham Act Waivers and Geopolitical Tensions
body: Oil prices have surged following President Trump's executive order on October 16, 2026, waiving the majority of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs introduced by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. While the waivers defer immediate new sanctions risks, the legislation provides a roadmap for future actions, creating market uncertainty.

The Graham Act had sought to codify existing executive order-based Russia sanctions, mandate new sanctions, and create new tariff authorities, including potential duties of up to 500 percent on goods from Russia and up to 100 percent on goods from top purchasers of Russian energy. The waivers, however, have temporarily eased immediate supply concerns related to these potential tariffs.

Despite the waivers, geopolitical tensions, particularly the ongoing conflict in Ukraine and the Middle Eastern crisis, continue to exert upward pressure on energy prices. The U.S. authorization of certain transactions related to imports of Russian diesel fuel until April 2027 also plays a role in the complex global energy market dynamics.

UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric stated that an attack not only on a place of worship but during a funeral procession is especially heinous. The Secretary-General expressed deep condolences to the families of the victims and wished a speedy recovery to all those injured.
The incident has raised concerns about security in the region and the protection of religious sites. Authorities in Jordan are investigating the circumstances surrounding the attack.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for October 2026, Including Penalties for BSA Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today released its enforcement actions for October 2026, targeting several banks for deficiencies in their Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance programs. These actions aim to ensure that financial institutions maintain robust anti-money laundering controls.

American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah, received a Cease and Desist Order and a Civil Money Penalty of $350 million for BSA compliance program deficiencies, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and customer due diligence and customer identification program violations.

Bank of America, National Association, Charlotte, North Carolina, was also assessed a Civil Money Penalty of $750 million for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. The OCC also issued Orders of Prohibition against individuals for embezzling customer funds.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

articles.headline: OCC Finalizes Stablecoin Rule with Narrower Interest Prohibition, Eyes Future Rulemaking
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has finalized a rule to enforce the Genius Act, which establishes a regulatory framework for payment stablecoins. The final rule includes a narrower prohibition on the payment of interest than initially proposed.

The Genius Act, passed last year, prohibits stablecoin issuers from offering yield or interest. While the OCC's final rule omits a proposed rebuttable presumption concerning certain payments involving affiliates and related third parties, it states that it will examine such arrangements on a case-by-case basis.

Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould stated that the OCC is providing a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management. The agency anticipates future rulemaking as the payment stablecoin market develops.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / Bank Policy Institute

articles.headline: OCC Report Finds Nine Major Banks Engaged in Debanking Practices
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released a report on October 14, 2026, titled 'Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans,' which concludes that nine of the largest national banks it supervises maintained policies or practices that may have influenced the denial or limitation of financial services based on customers' political or religious beliefs or lawful business activities.

The report, which reviewed nearly 100,000 complaints and approximately 50,000 documents from the banks, identified two broad categories of policies presenting an elevated risk of influencing debanking: general reputation risk policies and industry-specific restrictions (e.g., on Arctic oil and gas exploration, coal mining, firearms, tobacco, and digital asset activities).

Comptroller Jonathan Gould expressed a lack of confidence in the banks' current remedial efforts and indicated that the OCC will assess further changes to the regulatory and supervisory framework. This report signals a new phase in the federal debanking campaign, with potential concrete supervisory and enforcement consequences for banks.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / Ballotpedia News

articles.headline: OCC Imposes $750 Million Assessment Against Bank of America for Deficient BSA/AML Compliance
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. (bank), for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations, including 12 CFR 21.21 and 12 CFR 21.11. This amount is the largest in OCC history.

articles.headline: BIS Reaches Administrative Enforcement Settlement with Lambda Research Corporation
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has reached an administrative enforcement settlement with Lambda Research Corporation. This settlement addresses alleged violations of the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).

Details of the settlement, including the specific violations and any penalties imposed, are typically outlined in the official enforcement release. BIS regularly takes action against companies that fail to comply with U.S. export control laws.

This enforcement action serves as a reminder to companies involved in the export of sensitive technologies and goods to maintain robust compliance programs to prevent unauthorized transfers and adhere to EAR requirements.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
